# Docker Sandbox

Run your agent's commands and file edits in a local [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) or Podman container, created on first use, away from your machine's files and processes.

[Source](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/tree/main/src/pydantic_ai_harness/pydantic_ai_harness/docker_sandbox/)

> While Pydantic AI Harness is on 0.x releases, the API may change between minor releases; when it does, deprecation warnings and release-note migration guidance tell you (or your agent) exactly how to upgrade. See the [version policy](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/#version-policy).

## Install

uv:

```bash
uv add "pydantic-ai-harness[anthropic]"
```

pip:

```bash
pip install "pydantic-ai-harness[anthropic]"
```

No extra is needed for Docker itself: the capability runs the `docker` CLI already on your machine, so there is no SDK to install. The `anthropic` extra is there because the examples use an Anthropic model; swap it for your model provider's extra, and set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` for the examples.

## Quick start

```python {names="defined"}
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness.coder import Coder
from pydantic_ai_harness.docker_sandbox import DockerSandbox

agent = Agent('anthropic:claude-opus-5-5', capabilities=[DockerSandbox(image='python:3.13-slim'), Coder()])
result = agent.run_sync('Write a script that prints the first 10 primes, and run it.')
```

`Coder`'s shell and file tools now run in a container, not on your machine. The container is created on the run's first use of the workspace. With `Coder`, `RepoContext` uses it when the run starts, so use `Coder(repo_context=False)` to create it only when a tool needs it. The container keeps running after the run ends; see [Clean up](#clean-up).

The image needs a POSIX `sh` and the usual file utilities, and Docker pulls it the first time. Commands run as the image's user, usually `root`. They start in `/workspace`, which is created if it's missing.

A new container is on Docker's default bridge network, which reaches the internet, but also your local network and services on this machine. Pass `allow_internet_access=False` to run it with `--network none`.

## Continue in the same container

```python {names="defined"}
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness.coder import Coder
from pydantic_ai_harness.docker_sandbox import DockerSandbox

agent = Agent('anthropic:claude-opus-5-5', capabilities=[DockerSandbox(image='python:3.13-slim'), Coder()])
result = agent.run_sync('Write a script that prints the first 10 primes, and run it.')

followup = agent.run_sync('Now make it print the first 100.', message_history=result.all_messages())
```

The follow-up run finds the container in the message history and works in it, so the script is still there. Without the history, a run creates a new container. If the container has been removed, the run raises `WorkspaceUnavailableError` instead of starting over in an empty one.

## Choose the tools

For a narrower agent, use [`Shell`](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/shell/) and [`FileSystem`](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/filesystem/) instead of `Coder`, or write your own tool:

```python {names="defined"}
from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext
from pydantic_ai_harness.docker_sandbox import DockerSandbox
from pydantic_ai_harness.filesystem import FileSystem
from pydantic_ai_harness.shell import Shell

agent = Agent('anthropic:claude-opus-5-5', capabilities=[DockerSandbox(image='python:3.13-slim'), Shell(), FileSystem()])


@agent.tool
async def run_python(ctx: RunContext, code: str) -> str:
    """Run a Python snippet in the container."""
    result = await ctx.workspace.run(['python', '-c', code], timeout=10)
    return result.stdout + result.stderr
```

See [Workspaces](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/core-concepts/workspace/) for more.

## Work on a project directory

A new container starts empty. To let the agent work on a directory on your machine, mount it with `docker_args`, extra `docker run` arguments:

```python {names="defined"}
from pathlib import Path

from pydantic_ai_harness.docker_sandbox import DockerSandbox

project = Path('.').resolve()
sandbox = DockerSandbox(
    image='python:3.13-slim',
    docker_args=['--volume', f'{project}:/workspace', '--memory', '2g', '--cpus', '2'],
    allow_internet_access=False,
)
```

The mount is the only part of your machine's files the commands can change; the network is a separate setting. For a network of your own, leave `allow_internet_access` on and pass `--network` in `docker_args`, since Docker refuses a second `--network` next to `--network none`. `docker_args` can't change the container's name, its `ai.pydantic.workspace=true` label or its entrypoint. Set the directory commands start in with `working_dir`.

A new container gets `--pids-limit 2048`, so a runaway fork loop can't use up the process table of the machine (or VM) running Docker. A command that hits it fails with `Cannot fork` or `Resource temporarily unavailable`; pass your own `--pids-limit` in `docker_args` to change it, or `-1` to remove it.

## Use a remote Docker host

The capability runs the `docker` CLI on your machine, so it uses whichever daemon that CLI points at. To run containers on another host, point the CLI there before the agent starts; your code doesn't change:

```bash
export DOCKER_HOST=ssh://dev@build-box  # or: docker context use build-box
```

The host needs Docker, and `ssh` must log in without a prompt, through a key or your SSH agent. `DOCKER_HOST` overrides `DOCKER_CONTEXT`, which overrides `docker context use`, so unset the ones you don't use. Paths in `docker_args`, such as a `--volume` source, are paths on that host, and `allow_internet_access` reaches that host's network. Each run reads these settings when it starts, and `destroy` when it's called, so keep them the same while a container is in use.

## Reattach later

To come back to the container without the message history, store the run's workspace ref and pass it back as `workspace=`:

```python {names="defined"}
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai_harness.coder import Coder
from pydantic_ai_harness.docker_sandbox import DockerSandbox

agent = Agent('anthropic:claude-opus-5-5', capabilities=[DockerSandbox(image='python:3.13-slim'), Coder()])

result = agent.run_sync('Write a script that prints the first 10 primes, and run it.')
ref = result.workspace.ref  # store this, e.g. in your database

later = agent.run_sync('Now make it print the first 100.', workspace=ref)
```

The ref is `WorkspaceRef(provider='docker', id='pydantic-ai-<hex>')`, the container's name. Attaching starts a stopped container on first use, so it comes back with its files. Pass `workspace='new'` to create a fresh container even when the message history names one. `image`, `allow_internet_access` and `docker_args` only shape a new container. `working_dir` and `env` apply to every command.

A ref is trusted input: whoever passes one runs commands in that container. `DockerSandbox` refuses a container without its `ai.pydantic.workspace=true` label, so a ref can't reach the other containers the Docker daemon serves. The label isn't proof of origin, though: any `DockerSandbox` on this machine, or anyone who can run `docker`, can create a container with it, so only pass refs your application stored itself.

## Prepare a container before the run

To seed files or install packages before the agent starts, create the backend yourself, work in it through `Workspace`, and pass it to the run:

```python {names="defined"}
import asyncio

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from pydantic_ai.workspaces import Workspace
from pydantic_ai_harness.coder import Coder
from pydantic_ai_harness.docker_sandbox import DockerSandbox, DockerSandboxBackend

agent = Agent('anthropic:claude-opus-5-5', capabilities=[DockerSandbox(image='python:3.13-slim'), Coder()])


async def main() -> None:
    backend = DockerSandboxBackend(image='python:3.13-slim')
    try:
        workspace = Workspace(backend)
        await workspace.write_text('calc.py', 'def add(a, b):\n    return a - b\n')
        install = await workspace.run(['pip', 'install', 'pytest'], timeout=300)
        if install.exit_code != 0:
            raise RuntimeError(f'pip install failed: {install.stderr}')
        result = await agent.run('Fix the bug in calc.py.', workspace=backend)
        print(result.output)
    finally:
        ref = backend.ref  # set once the container is being created
        if ref is not None:
            await DockerSandbox().destroy(ref)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    asyncio.run(main())
```

The `finally` removes the container even when setup or the run fails. To keep it instead, store `backend.ref` and pass it as `workspace=` to reattach later. `DockerSandbox`'s settings don't apply to a backend you pass as `workspace=`; give the backend its own.

## Clean up

A run never removes its container. Remove it, with its anonymous volumes, with the ref you stored:

```python {names="defined"}
from pydantic_ai.workspaces import WorkspaceRef
from pydantic_ai_harness.docker_sandbox import DockerSandbox


async def remove_container(ref: WorkspaceRef) -> None:
    await DockerSandbox().destroy(ref)
```

Removing a container that is already gone returns quietly. `DockerSandbox()` without an `image` attaches to and removes containers by ref, and leaves a run without a ref to the agent's other workspace capabilities.

Nothing removes a container for you, and there is no idle or lifetime limit. `docker ps --all --filter label=ai.pydantic.workspace=true` finds the containers `DockerSandbox` created, including any left behind without a stored ref.

`backend.ref` is set when the first operation starts creating the container, and goes back to `None` if creating it fails before a container exists. If the create is cancelled, Docker may still finish creating the container after `destroy` has found nothing to remove; the label filter above finds it. A failed run returns no result, so there is no ref to store. Remove the container in an `on_run_error` hook, as shown for [E2B](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/e2b-sandbox/#clean-up), or create the backend yourself as in [Prepare a container before the run](#prepare-a-container-before-the-run).

## How commands run

The container doesn't run the image's own entrypoint or command, so a service the image would start on boot isn't running; start it with a command. Creating or starting the container, including pulling the image, is not bounded by a command's `timeout`. File operations run as commands in the container, so large files are slow to read and write: mount a directory with `docker_args` for large data.

A container that can't be created or started, or that stops mid-command, raises `WorkspaceUnavailableError`. The exit code is the command's own, even when it is one `docker` also uses for its own errors.

On a timeout or cancellation, the command and the processes it started are stopped in the container; a command that detached into a session of its own, like a [Shell](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/shell/) background job, keeps running.

With Docker, a command that leaves a background process holding its output open, such as `server &` without redirecting the server's output, doesn't return until that process exits: redirect it, as in `server > server.log 2>&1 &`. With Podman, it returns when the command itself exits.

Podman works too: pass `executable='podman'`. The CLI is looked up on `PATH` once, when the capability or backend is created. The `docker` client gets `DOCKER_HOST`, `DOCKER_CONTEXT`, `DOCKER_CONFIG`, `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` and the other variables that select and reach a daemon from your environment, besides the `PATH`, `HOME` and locale every local command gets, and nothing else from it.

## Security model

A container shares your machine's kernel, so it is a weaker boundary than a VM such as [Smol Sandbox](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/smol-sandbox/), [E2B](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/e2b-sandbox/) or [Modal](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/modal-sandbox/). Inside, commands run as the image's user, usually `root`, so anything the agent runs can change anything in the container.

- Don't mount the Docker socket or directories holding secrets. A writable mount also lets commands change files your machine runs later, such as a virtualenv, the `docker` CLI inside one, or git hooks. Add hardening such as `--cap-drop ALL`, `--user` or `--read-only` through `docker_args` when the image allows it.
- A missing `working_dir` is created as the container's user, so with `--user`, point `working_dir` at a directory that user can write, such as a mount, or pass `working_dir=None` to use the image's own. With `--read-only`, mount a writable working directory.
- On Linux, files the commands write to a mounted directory belong to the container's user on your machine too, which is `root` unless you pass `--user` with your own IDs, such as `--user 1000:1000` from `id -u` and `id -g`.
- While a command runs, its `env` values are visible in process listings (`ps`) on your machine.
- Docker adds the proxy settings in your `~/.docker/config.json` to every new container as environment variables.
- `image` is pulled by tag; pin a digest, such as `python:3.13-slim@sha256:...`, to get the same image every time.

## Configuration

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `image` | Image for a new container, such as `'python:3.13-slim'`. Default: `None`, which only attaches to and removes containers by ref. |
| `working_dir` | Absolute directory commands start in and relative paths resolve against, created on first use if missing. Default: `/workspace`; `None` uses the image's own (`WORKDIR`, or `/`). |
| `env` | Environment variables every command gets, on top of the image's. Default: `None`. Nothing from your machine's environment reaches the container except Docker's proxy settings, and `env` is kept out of the capability's `repr`, but the agent's commands can read it. |
| `allow_internet_access` | Whether a new container gets outbound network access, through Docker's default bridge. Default: `True`; `False` runs it with `--network none`. |
| `docker_args` | Extra `docker run` arguments for a new container, such as mounts, `--memory` or `--user`; a `--pids-limit` here replaces the default of 2048. Default: `()`. |
| `executable` | The container CLI to run, such as `'podman'`, looked up on `PATH` when the capability is created. Default: `'docker'`. |

## Platforms

The machine running the agent must be POSIX (Linux or macOS), like [`LocalWorkspace`](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/core-concepts/workspace/#platforms). On Windows, `DockerSandboxBackend` raises `NotImplementedError` when it is constructed, so a run with `DockerSandbox` does too.

## Telemetry

`DockerSandbox` emits no spans of its own. Core's [instrumentation](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/capabilities/instrumentation/) records the container on the agent run span as `pydantic_ai.workspace.provider` (`docker`) and `pydantic_ai.workspace.id` (its name). Each command or file operation a tool makes runs inside that tool call's span.

# Citations

A citation tells you which source backs up part of a model's answer: a web page it searched or fetched, a document
you sent, or a file in a provider's file store.

Pydantic AI puts citations on [`TextPart.citations`][pydantic_ai.messages.TextPart.citations], in the same shape for
every provider. The model's text is never changed.

## Turning citations on

Most models cite the results of search tools, such as [web search](native-tools.md#web-search-tool),
[web fetch](native-tools.md#web-fetch-tool) and [file search](native-tools.md#file-search-tool), without being asked.
Some providers only cite the documents you send, or on xAI any source, when you ask. Add the [`Citations`][pydantic_ai.capabilities.Citations]
capability to ask them:

```python {title="document_citations.py"}
from pydantic_ai import Agent, BinaryContent, TextPart
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import Citations

agent = Agent('{{ anthropic:medium }}', capabilities=[Citations()])
result = agent.run_sync(
    [
        'How long do customers have to return an item?',
        BinaryContent(data=b'Items may be returned within 30 days.', media_type='text/plain'),
    ]
)
for part in result.response.parts:
    if isinstance(part, TextPart):
        for citation in part.citations or []:
            print(citation.sources[0].excerpts)
            #> ['Items may be returned within 30 days.']
```

The model can still answer without citations.

## Reading citations

A [`Citation`][pydantic_ai.messages.Citation] has:

- `sources`: where the information came from. A [`WebCitationSource`][pydantic_ai.messages.WebCitationSource] has the
  page's `url`. A [`DocumentCitationSource`][pydantic_ai.messages.DocumentCitationSource] is any other source. Its
  `document_id` is the provider's ID, not a file path, and a document you sent in the prompt may have no ID or title.
  Each source's `excerpts` are the passages the provider quoted as evidence. Several sources on one citation are the
  ones the provider grouped together; they may copy each other, so their number says nothing about how well the text
  is supported.
- `anchor`: the part of the text the citation is about, as character positions: `part.content[anchor.start:anchor.end]`.
    - A [`ContentCitationAnchor`][pydantic_ai.messages.ContentCitationAnchor] covers the text the sources support.
      Some providers, such as Anthropic, cite whole text parts, so the anchor covers the whole part.
    - A [`MarkerCitationAnchor`][pydantic_ai.messages.MarkerCitationAnchor] covers a marker the model wrote, such as
      `[1]` or a link.
    - `None` means the provider didn't say which text the citation is about. OpenAI file citations, for example, only
      give a position, which is kept in the part's `provider_details['citations']`.

```python {title="render_citations.py"}
from pydantic_ai import (
    Agent,
    ContentCitationAnchor,
    MarkerCitationAnchor,
    TextPart,
    WebCitationSource,
)
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import NativeTool
from pydantic_ai.native_tools import WebSearchTool

agent = Agent('{{ openai:medium }}', capabilities=[NativeTool(WebSearchTool())])
result = agent.run_sync('What is the tallest mountain in Alberta?')

for part in result.response.parts:
    if isinstance(part, TextPart):
        for citation in part.citations or []:
            anchor = citation.anchor
            if isinstance(anchor, ContentCitationAnchor):
                location = f'supports {part.content[anchor.start : anchor.end]!r}'
            elif isinstance(anchor, MarkerCitationAnchor):
                location = f'marker {part.content[anchor.start : anchor.end]!r}'
            else:
                location = 'somewhere in the text'

            for source in citation.sources:
                if isinstance(source, WebCitationSource):
                    label = source.title or source.url
                else:
                    label = source.title or source.document_id or 'document'
                print(location, label)
                #> marker '([example.com](https://example.com))' Mount Columbia
```

The same answer looks like this from different providers:

```python
from pydantic_ai import (
    Citation,
    ContentCitationAnchor,
    MarkerCitationAnchor,
    TextPart,
    WebCitationSource,
)

# Google selects the supported text, and here lists both sources for it. Anthropic's anchor covers the whole part.
TextPart(
    'Pydantic validates data.',
    citations=[
        Citation(
            sources=[WebCitationSource('https://a.example'), WebCitationSource('https://b.example')],
            anchor=ContentCitationAnchor(start=0, end=24),
        )
    ],
)

# OpenAI selects the link the model wrote.
TextPart(
    'Pydantic validates data. ([example.com](https://example.com))',
    citations=[
        Citation(
            sources=[WebCitationSource('https://example.com')],
            anchor=MarkerCitationAnchor(start=25, end=61),
        )
    ],
)

# Some providers give no position in the text.
TextPart(
    'Pydantic validates data.',
    citations=[Citation(sources=[WebCitationSource('https://example.com')])],
)
```

## Citations, tools and structured output

Citations are attached to text, so they only come back when your agent's output is text. With
[structured output](output.md), including an output type that combines `str` with a structured type, such as
`[str, Answer]`, the answer comes back as tool call arguments, which can't carry citations.

On Anthropic, and on Bedrock with Anthropic models, the model writes its citation markup into anything that isn't
text, such as `summary='<cite index="1-1">Items may be returned within 30 days.</cite>'`. So with
`Citations()`:

- **Structured output:** the model isn't asked for citations, so your fields stay clean and you get no document
  citations. (Anthropic rejects citations with `NativeOutput`.)
- **A tool call forced with [`tool_choice`](tools-advanced.md#dynamic-tool-choice-via-capabilities), in a request
  with a document or Web Fetch:** raises a `UserError` before that request is sent, because the markup reaches the
  tool's arguments every time. A run that forces a tool on a later step fails at that step.
- **Tools the model chooses to call:** citations stay on, but smaller models often write the markup into the tool's
  arguments, about half the time in our tests when the arguments summarise a document. Check arguments that end up
  in front of people, such as an email body, or leave `Citations()` off for those agents.

On xAI, the model answers in text instead of calling the output tool when citations are on, so with structured output
`Citations()` doesn't ask for them either. Tools work as usual.

If you need citations, use text output.

Anthropic always cites [web search](native-tools.md#web-search-tool) results, so with web search the markup can show
up in structured output even without `Citations()`. The same goes for [web fetch](native-tools.md#web-fetch-tool)
when you set `enable_citations=True` on the tool.

On other providers, `Citations()` has no effect on structured output. With `NativeOutput` or `PromptedOutput` the
output is JSON text, so web search citations can come back on it, with positions in the JSON text rather than in your
fields.

## Good to know

- When streaming, citations can arrive after their text: at the end of each text part on Anthropic, Bedrock and
  OpenAI Responses, and at the end of the response on Google and OpenAI Chat. Read citations from the final response.
  On xAI they go on the last text part at the end of the response, so a streamed answer followed by a tool call gets
  none.
- The [AG-UI adapter](ui/ag-ui.md) doesn't send citations to the frontend.
- Citation URLs, titles and excerpts come from the sources themselves, and excerpts can include text from your own
  documents. Check them before you log them or show them to users.
- Anything else the provider returned about a citation, such as Google's confidence scores, is kept as the provider
  sent it in the part's `provider_details['citations']`. Its shape is the provider's and can change.

## Citations in message history

[Saved message history](message-history.md#storing-and-loading-messages-to-json) keeps every citation. When you send
it back to the same provider, these citations go with the text, so the model knows where its earlier statements came
from:

| Provider | Citations sent back |
| --- | --- |
| Anthropic | Web search citations, except on clients without web search, such as Bedrock |
| OpenAI Responses | Web and file citations, when message IDs are sent, which is the default for reasoning models. See [`openai_send_reasoning_ids`][pydantic_ai.models.openai.OpenAIResponsesModelSettings.openai_send_reasoning_ids] |

Every other citation stays on the saved messages, but its text goes back as plain text: document and fetched-page
citations, citations from OpenAI Chat, and history sent to a different provider. So does a citation whose text was
changed or joined with other text.

If you edit the text of a saved answer, also clear that part's `citations` and its `provider_details['citations']`.
Pydantic AI leaves out citations whose text clearly changed, but an edit that keeps the same length can go unnoticed.

History that's sent back unchanged goes out the same way every turn, so prompt caching keeps working.

The [Vercel AI adapter](ui/vercel-ai.md#citations) keeps citations when the frontend holds the message history.

!!! warning "The model may not see the source"
    If a user later asks about "source [1]", the model may see the `[1]` but not what it pointed to. Put the source in
    the new prompt, or let the model look it up again.

## Provider support

| Provider | Citations | How to turn them on | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations) | Web search, web fetch and documents | Web search: always. Web fetch and documents, including documents returned by tools: `Citations()`. [`WebFetchTool(enable_citations=True)`][pydantic_ai.native_tools.WebFetchTool.enable_citations] turns them on for web fetch only | Anchors cover whole text parts. A fetched PDF is a document source. Citations of search results you provide yourself aren't included |
| [Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_CitationsContentBlock.html) | Documents, on Anthropic models | `Citations()`, for text and PDF documents, including documents returned by tools | Other models on Bedrock don't support citations, so they ignore the setting. Anchors cover whole text parts. A document's title is the name Pydantic AI gives it, such as `Document 1`. Documents read from S3 aren't cited, as Bedrock doesn't allow it. With citations on, a text document must be UTF-8, or Pydantic AI raises a `UserError` |
| [Google Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/google-search) | Google Search, file search and web fetch | Turn on the tool | Google Search URLs are Google redirect links, and titles are often just the site's domain |
| [Google Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/grounding/overview) | Google Search | Turn on the tool | Same as the Gemini API |
| [OpenAI Chat and Responses](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/tools-web-search) | Web pages, and files on Responses | Turn on web search, or file search for files | Other annotation types, such as `container_file_citation`, are only available with [`openai_include_raw_annotations`][pydantic_ai.models.openai.OpenAIChatModelSettings.openai_include_raw_annotations] |
| [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/web-search) | Web pages | Turn on web search. Perplexity Sonar models always search, and OpenRouter rejects them with the web search tool | OpenRouter doesn't say where in the text a citation belongs, so citations have no anchor |
| [xAI](https://docs.x.ai/developers/tools/citations) | Web, X and collection citations | `Citations()`, with a search tool such as web search or X search | Turning citations on changes the answer: the model writes Markdown markers such as `[[1]](https://x.com/...)` into it, and the anchor covers the marker. Collection citations are document sources |

# Dependencies

Pydantic AI uses a dependency injection system to provide data and services to your agent's [instructions](agent.md#instructions), [tools](tools.md) and [output validators](output.md#output-validator-functions).

Pydantic AI's dependency system follows established Python practices, making dependencies type-safe, understandable, easy to test, and easy to deploy in production.

## Defining Dependencies

Dependencies can be any python type. While in simple cases you might be able to pass a single object as a dependency (e.g. an HTTP connection), [dataclasses][] are generally a convenient container when your dependencies include multiple objects.

Here's an example of defining an agent that requires dependencies.

(**Note:** dependencies aren't actually used in this example, see [Accessing Dependencies](#accessing-dependencies) below)

```python {title="unused_dependencies.py"}
from dataclasses import dataclass

import httpx

from pydantic_ai import Agent


@dataclass
class MyDeps:  # (1)!
    api_key: str
    http_client: httpx.AsyncClient


agent = Agent(
    '{{ openai:medium }}',
    deps_type=MyDeps,  # (2)!
)


async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        deps = MyDeps('foobar', client)
        result = await agent.run(
            'Tell me a joke.',
            deps=deps,  # (3)!
        )
        print(result.output)
        #> Did you hear about the toothpaste scandal? They called it Colgate.
```

1. Define a dataclass to hold dependencies.
2. Pass the dataclass type to the `deps_type` argument of the [`Agent` constructor][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.__init__]. **Note**: we're passing the type here, NOT an instance, this parameter is not actually used at runtime, it's here so we can get full type checking of the agent.
3. When running the agent, pass an instance of the dataclass to the `deps` parameter.

_(To run this example, ensure `asyncio` is imported and add `asyncio.run(main())`; no other changes are needed.)_

## Accessing Dependencies

Dependencies are accessed through the [`RunContext`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext] type, this should be the first parameter of instructions functions etc.

```python {title="instructions_dependencies.py" hl_lines="20-27"}
from dataclasses import dataclass

import httpx

from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext


@dataclass
class MyDeps:
    api_key: str
    http_client: httpx.AsyncClient


agent = Agent(
    '{{ openai:medium }}',
    deps_type=MyDeps,
)


@agent.instructions  # (1)!
async def get_instructions(ctx: RunContext[MyDeps]) -> str:  # (2)!
    response = await ctx.deps.http_client.get(  # (3)!
        'https://example.com',
        headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {ctx.deps.api_key}'},  # (4)!
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return f'Prompt: {response.text}'


async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        deps = MyDeps('foobar', client)
        result = await agent.run('Tell me a joke.', deps=deps)
        print(result.output)
        #> Did you hear about the toothpaste scandal? They called it Colgate.
```

1. [`RunContext`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext] may optionally be passed to an [`instructions`][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.instructions] function as the only argument.
2. [`RunContext`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext] is parameterized with the type of the dependencies, if this type is incorrect, static type checkers will raise an error.
3. Access the HTTP client through the [`.deps`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext.deps] attribute.
4. Access the API key through the same attribute.

_(To run this example, ensure `asyncio` is imported and add `asyncio.run(main())`; no other changes are needed.)_

In addition to [`.deps`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext.deps], [`RunContext`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext] provides access to the running agent via [`.agent`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext.agent], which is useful when [tools](tools.md), [hooks](hooks.md), or [capabilities](capabilities/overview.md) need to read agent properties like [`name`][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.name] or [`output_type`][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.output_type]. The [`.realtime`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext.realtime] property identifies realtime sessions without requiring a model type check, and [`.realtime_session`][pydantic_ai.tools.RunContext.realtime_session] exposes the live [`RealtimeSession`][pydantic_ai.realtime.RealtimeSession] to tools and hooks once it is connected.

Dependency fields can also be referenced in instructions and descriptions via [template strings](agent-spec.md#template-strings) — for example, [`TemplateStr('Hello {{name}}')`][pydantic_ai.template.TemplateStr] renders `name` from the deps object at runtime. This is especially useful in [agent specs](agent-spec.md) where callables aren't available.

### Asynchronous vs. Synchronous dependencies

[Instructions functions](agent.md#instructions), [function tools](tools.md) and [output validators](output.md#output-validator-functions) are all run in the async context of an agent run.

If these functions are synchronous, defined with `def` rather than `async def`, Pydantic AI calls them with
[`run_in_executor`][asyncio.loop.run_in_executor] in a thread pool. Prefer `async` functions when dependencies
perform I/O, although synchronous dependencies also work.

!!! note "`run` vs. `run_sync` and Asynchronous vs. Synchronous dependencies"
    Whether you use synchronous or asynchronous dependencies is completely independent of whether you use `run` or `run_sync` — `run_sync` is just a wrapper around `run` and agents are always run in an async context.

Here's the same example as above, but with a synchronous dependency:

```python {title="sync_dependencies.py"}
from dataclasses import dataclass

import httpx

from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext


@dataclass
class MyDeps:
    api_key: str
    http_client: httpx.Client  # (1)!


agent = Agent(
    '{{ openai:medium }}',
    deps_type=MyDeps,
)


@agent.instructions
def get_instructions(ctx: RunContext[MyDeps]) -> str:  # (2)!
    response = ctx.deps.http_client.get(
        'https://example.com', headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {ctx.deps.api_key}'}
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return f'Prompt: {response.text}'


async def main():
    deps = MyDeps('foobar', httpx.Client())
    result = await agent.run(
        'Tell me a joke.',
        deps=deps,
    )
    print(result.output)
    #> Did you hear about the toothpaste scandal? They called it Colgate.
```

1. Here we use a synchronous `httpx.Client` instead of an asynchronous `httpx.AsyncClient`.
2. To match the synchronous dependency, the instructions function is now a plain function, not a coroutine.

_(To run this example, ensure `asyncio` is imported and add `asyncio.run(main())`; no other changes are needed.)_

## Full Example

As well as instructions, dependencies can be used in [tools](tools.md) and [output validators](output.md#output-validator-functions).

```python {title="full_example.py" hl_lines="27-35 38-48"}
from dataclasses import dataclass

import httpx

from pydantic_ai import Agent, ModelRetry, RunContext


@dataclass
class MyDeps:
    api_key: str
    http_client: httpx.AsyncClient


agent = Agent(
    '{{ openai:medium }}',
    deps_type=MyDeps,
)


@agent.instructions
async def get_instructions(ctx: RunContext[MyDeps]) -> str:
    response = await ctx.deps.http_client.get('https://example.com')
    response.raise_for_status()
    return f'Prompt: {response.text}'


@agent.tool  # (1)!
async def get_joke_material(ctx: RunContext[MyDeps], subject: str) -> str:
    response = await ctx.deps.http_client.get(
        'https://example.com#jokes',
        params={'subject': subject},
        headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {ctx.deps.api_key}'},
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.text


@agent.output_validator  # (2)!
async def validate_output(ctx: RunContext[MyDeps], output: str) -> str:
    response = await ctx.deps.http_client.post(
        'https://example.com#validate',
        headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {ctx.deps.api_key}'},
        params={'query': output},
    )
    if response.status_code == 400:
        raise ModelRetry(f'invalid response: {response.text}')
    response.raise_for_status()
    return output


async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        deps = MyDeps('foobar', client)
        result = await agent.run('Tell me a joke.', deps=deps)
        print(result.output)
        #> Did you hear about the toothpaste scandal? They called it Colgate.
```

1. To pass `RunContext` to a tool, use the [`tool`][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.tool] decorator.
2. `RunContext` may optionally be passed to a [`output_validator`][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.output_validator] function as the first argument.

_(To run this example, ensure `asyncio` is imported and add `asyncio.run(main())`; no other changes are needed.)_

## Overriding Dependencies

When testing agents, it's useful to be able to customise dependencies.

While this can sometimes be done by calling the agent directly within unit tests, we can also override dependencies
while calling application code which in turn calls the agent.

This is done via the [`override`][pydantic_ai.agent.Agent.override] method on the agent.

```python {title="joke_app.py"}
from dataclasses import dataclass

import httpx

from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext


@dataclass
class MyDeps:
    api_key: str
    http_client: httpx.AsyncClient

    async def instructions_factory(self) -> str:  # (1)!
        response = await self.http_client.get('https://example.com')
        response.raise_for_status()
        return f'Prompt: {response.text}'


joke_agent = Agent('{{ openai:medium }}', deps_type=MyDeps)


@joke_agent.instructions
async def get_instructions(ctx: RunContext[MyDeps]) -> str:
    return await ctx.deps.instructions_factory()  # (2)!


async def application_code(prompt: str) -> str:  # (3)!
    ...
    ...
    # now deep within application code we call our agent
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        app_deps = MyDeps('foobar', client)
        result = await joke_agent.run(prompt, deps=app_deps)  # (4)!
    return result.output
```

1. Define a method on the dependency to make the instructions easier to customise.
2. Call the instructions factory from within the instructions function.
3. Application code that calls the agent, in a real application this might be an API endpoint.
4. Call the agent from within the application code, in a real application this call might be deep within a call stack. Note `app_deps` here will NOT be used when deps are overridden.

_(This example is complete, it can be run "as is")_

```python {title="test_joke_app.py" hl_lines="12-14" call_name="test_application_code" requires="joke_app.py"}
import httpx

from joke_app import MyDeps, application_code, joke_agent


class TestMyDeps(MyDeps):  # (1)!
    async def instructions_factory(self) -> str:
        return 'test prompt'


async def test_application_code():
    test_deps = TestMyDeps('test_key', httpx.AsyncClient())  # (2)!
    with joke_agent.override(deps=test_deps):  # (3)!
        joke = await application_code('Tell me a joke.')  # (4)!
    assert joke.startswith('Did you hear about the toothpaste scandal?')
```

1. Define a subclass of `MyDeps` in tests to customise the instructions factory.
2. Create an instance of the test dependency. Its `http_client` goes unused, as the test instructions factory makes no requests.
3. Override the dependencies of the agent for the duration of the `with` block, `test_deps` will be used when the agent is run.
4. Now we can safely call our application code, the agent will use the overridden dependencies.

# Migrate to Pydantic AI

If you have an application built with another agent framework, your coding agent can use a migration skill bundled with Pydantic AI. Each skill helps the agent understand the source framework, choose the right Pydantic AI components, and port one working application path at a time.

The skills preserve behavior rather than translating API names one for one. They separate responsibilities between:

- [Pydantic AI](agent.md) for agents, models, tools, outputs, messages, and streaming;
- [Pydantic Graph](graph.md) for explicit application control flow;
- [Pydantic AI Harness](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/) for optional capabilities such as skills, memory, subagents, planning, and sandboxed tools;
- [Pydantic Evals](evals.md) for evaluation datasets and checks;
- your application for authentication, storage, APIs, UI, deployment, and other product infrastructure.

## Supported source frameworks

| Source framework | Migration skill |
|---|---|
| [LangChain and LangGraph](comparisons/vs-langchain-langgraph.md) | `migrating-langchain-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Agno](comparisons/vs-agno.md) | `migrating-agno-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Claude Agent SDK](comparisons/vs-claude-agent-sdk.md) | `migrating-claude-agent-sdk-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Google Agent Development Kit](comparisons/vs-google-adk.md) | `migrating-google-adk-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Mastra](comparisons/vs-mastra.md) | `migrating-mastra-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [OpenAI Agents SDK](comparisons/vs-openai-agents-sdk.md) | `migrating-openai-agents-sdk-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Pi](comparisons/vs-pi.md) | `migrating-pi-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Vercel AI SDK and Eve](comparisons/vs-vercel-ai-sdk.md) | `migrating-vercel-ai-sdk-and-eve-to-pydantic-ai` |

## Use a migration skill

Install the skills bundled with your project dependencies:

```bash
uvx library-skills --all
```

See [Coding Agent Skills](coding-agent-skills.md#library-skills) for installation details, including Claude Code support.

Then open your existing application in your coding agent and name the matching skill in your request. For example:

```text
Use the migrating-openai-agents-sdk-to-pydantic-ai skill to migrate this application
to Pydantic AI. Preserve its existing API and behavior, and verify the port with tests.
```

The coding agent should first trace a real request through the source application and record what callers observe. It can then migrate the smallest complete path, test the old and new behavior at the same boundary, and explain any difference that cannot be preserved exactly. Remove the old framework only after every required path has been verified.

# Version Policy

Pydantic AI V1 was released in September 2025, and the stable V2.0 was released on June 23, 2026; see the [Upgrade Guide](changelog.md) for what's in V2, how to install it, and how to upgrade.

We will not intentionally make breaking changes in minor releases. Functionality marked as deprecated in a release is not removed until the next major version, which we won't release sooner than 3 months after V2.0.

We'll continue to provide security fixes for V1 for at least 6 months after V2's stable release, so you have time to upgrade your applications. When you're ready to make the jump, the [Upgrade Guide](changelog.md) lists the breaking changes for each version, along with our recommended path to V2.

Of course, some apparently safe changes and bug fixes will inevitably break some users' code — obligatory link to [xkcd](https://xkcd.com/1172/).

The following changes will **NOT** be considered breaking changes, and may occur in minor releases:

* Bug fixes that may result in existing code breaking, provided that such code was relying on undocumented features/constructs/assumptions.
* Adding new [message parts][pydantic_ai.messages], [stream events][pydantic_ai.messages.AgentStreamEvent], or optional fields (including fields with default values) on existing message (part) and event types. Always code defensively when consuming message parts or event streams, and use the [`ModelMessagesTypeAdapter`][pydantic_ai.messages.ModelMessagesTypeAdapter] to (de)serialize message histories.
* Changing OpenTelemetry span attributes. Because different [observability platforms](logfire.md#using-opentelemetry) support different versions of the [OpenTelemetry Semantic Conventions for Generative AI systems](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/), Pydantic AI lets you configure the [instrumentation version](logfire.md#configuring-data-format), but the default version may change in a minor release. Span attributes for [Pydantic Evals](evals.md) may also change as we iterate on Evals support in [Pydantic Logfire](https://logfire.pydantic.dev/docs/guides/web-ui/evals/).
* Changing how `__repr__` behaves, even of public classes.
* Adding or removing model names in the `Literal` type aliases that list known model names, such as [`KnownModelName`][pydantic_ai.models.KnownModelName]. They exist for IDE autocompletion.

In all cases we will aim to minimize churn and do so only when justified by the increase of quality of Pydantic AI for users.

When one of these permitted changes requires existing code to change, its pull request and release note will include a prominent **compatibility impact** warning and migration guidance.

## Beta Features

At Pydantic, we like to move quickly and innovate! To that end, minor releases may introduce beta features (indicated by a `beta` module) that are active works in progress. While in its beta phase, a feature's API and behaviors may not be stable, and it's very possible that changes made to the feature will not be backward-compatible. We aim to move beta features out of beta within a few months after initial release, once users have had a chance to provide feedback and test the feature in production.

## Support for Python versions

Pydantic will drop support for a Python version when the following conditions are met:

* The Python version has reached its [expected end of life](https://devguide.python.org/versions/).
* less than 5% of downloads of the most recent minor release are using that version.

# Pydantic Evals [![CI](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?event=push)](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/actions/workflows/ci.yml?query=branch%3Amain) ![Coverage](https://coverage-badge.samuelcolvin.workers.dev/pydantic/pydantic-ai.svg) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/pydantic-evals.svg)](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/pydantic-evals) [![python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/pydantic-evals.svg)](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai) [![license](https://img.shields.io/github/license/pydantic/pydantic-ai.svg)](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/blob/main/LICENSE) This is a library for evaluating non-deterministic (or "stochastic") functions in Python. It provides a simple, Pythonic interface for defining and running stochastic functions, and analyzing the results of running those functions. While this library is developed as part of [Pydantic AI](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/), it only uses Pydantic AI for a small subset of generative functionality internally, and it is designed to be used with arbitrary "stochastic function" implementations. In particular, it can be used with other (non-Pydantic AI) AI libraries, agent frameworks, etc. As with Pydantic AI, this library prioritizes type safety and use of common Python syntax over esoteric, domain-specific use of Python syntax. Full documentation is available at [pydantic.dev/docs/ai/evals](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/evals/evals/). ## Example While you'd typically use Pydantic Evals with more complex functions (such as Pydantic AI agents or graphs), here's a quick example that evaluates a simple function against a test case using both custom and built-in evaluators: ```python from pydantic_evals import Case, Dataset from pydantic_evals.evaluators import Evaluator, EvaluatorContext, IsInstance # Define a test case with inputs and expected output case = Case( name='capital_question', inputs='What is the capital of France?', expected_output='Paris', ) # Define a custom evaluator class MatchAnswer(Evaluator[str, str]): def evaluate(self, ctx: EvaluatorContext[str, str]) -> float: if ctx.output == ctx.expected_output: return 1.0 elif ctx.expected_output is not None and ctx.expected_output.lower() in ctx.output.lower(): return 0.8 return 0.0 # Create a dataset with the test case and evaluators dataset = Dataset( name='capital_eval', cases=[case], evaluators=[IsInstance(type_name='str'), MatchAnswer()], ) # Define the function to evaluate async def answer_question(question: str) -> str: return 'Paris' # Run the evaluation report = dataset.evaluate_sync(answer_question) report.print(include_input=True, include_output=True) """ Evaluation Summary: answer_question ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┓ ┃ Case ID ┃ Inputs ┃ Outputs ┃ Scores ┃ Assertions ┃ Duration ┃ ┡━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━┩ │ capital_question │ What is the capital of France? │ Paris │ MatchAnswer: 1.00 │ ✔ │ 10ms │ ├──────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼───────────────────┼────────────┼──────────┤ │ Averages │ │ │ MatchAnswer: 1.00 │ 100.0% ✔ │ 10ms │ └──────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┴─────────┴───────────────────┴────────────┴──────────┘ """ ``` Using the library with more complex functions, such as Pydantic AI agents, is similar — all you need to do is define a task function wrapping the function you want to evaluate, with a signature that matches the inputs and outputs of your test cases. ## Logfire Integration Pydantic Evals uses OpenTelemetry to record traces for each case in your evaluations. You can send these traces to any OpenTelemetry-compatible backend. For the best experience, we recommend [Pydantic Logfire](https://logfire.pydantic.dev/docs), which includes custom views for evals:
You'll see full details about the inputs, outputs, token usage, execution durations, etc. And you'll have access to the full trace for each case — ideal for debugging, writing path-aware evaluators, or running the similar evaluations against production traces. Basic setup: ```python {test="skip" lint="skip" format="skip"} import logfire logfire.configure( send_to_logfire='if-token-present', environment='development', service_name='evals', ) ... my_dataset.evaluate_sync(my_task) ``` [Read more about the Logfire integration here.](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/evals/how-to/logfire-integration/)

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

import pytest
import yaml
from pydantic import TypeAdapter
from typing_extensions import TypedDict

WORKFLOW = Path(__file__).parents[1] / 'workflows' / 'pydantic-ai-ui-security-review.md'


class DetectStep(TypedDict):
    """A step in the detector job."""

    name: str
    run: str


class DetectJob(TypedDict):
    """The detector job definition."""

    steps: list[DetectStep]


class Workflow(TypedDict):
    """The workflow frontmatter fields used by these tests."""

    jobs: dict[str, object]


WORKFLOW_ADAPTER: TypeAdapter[Workflow] = TypeAdapter(Workflow)
DETECT_JOB_ADAPTER: TypeAdapter[DetectJob] = TypeAdapter(DetectJob)


def _detect(
    tmp_path: Path,
    changed_files: list[tuple[str, str]],
    *,
    files_api_fails: bool = False,
) -> str:
    source = WORKFLOW.read_text(encoding='utf-8')
    frontmatter = source.split('---', maxsplit=2)[1]
    workflow = WORKFLOW_ADAPTER.validate_python(yaml.safe_load(frontmatter))
    detect_job = DETECT_JOB_ADAPTER.validate_python(workflow['jobs']['detect'])
    run = next(step['run'] for step in detect_job['steps'] if step['name'] == 'Detect UI security paths in the PR')

    gh = tmp_path / 'gh'
    gh.write_text(
        """#!/usr/bin/env bash
if [[ "$*" == *"pulls/$PR_NUMBER/files"* ]]; then
  [[ "$*" == *"--paginate"* ]] || exit 3
  [[ "${GH_FILES_API_FAILURE:-false}" != true ]] || exit 1
  if [[ "$*" == *"@tsv"* ]]; then
    cat "$GH_CHANGED_FILES_FILE"
  else
    while IFS=$'\t' read -r filename previous; do
      [[ -n "$filename" ]] || continue
      printf '%s\n' "$filename"
      if [[ -n "$previous" ]]; then
        printf '%s\n' "$previous"
      fi
    done < "$GH_CHANGED_FILES_FILE"
  fi
else
  exit 2
fi
""",
        encoding='utf-8',
    )
    gh.chmod(0o755)

    output = tmp_path / 'github-output'
    changed_files_file = tmp_path / 'changed-files.tsv'
    changed_files_file.write_text('\n'.join(f'{new}\t{old}' for new, old in changed_files) + '\n', encoding='utf-8')
    process = subprocess.run(
        ['bash', '-e', '-c', run],
        env={
            **os.environ,
            'PATH': f'{tmp_path}:{os.environ["PATH"]}',
            'GITHUB_OUTPUT': str(output),
            'GH_TOKEN': 'test-token',
            'PR_NUMBER': '123',
            'REPO': 'pydantic/pydantic-ai',
            'GH_CHANGED_FILES_FILE': str(changed_files_file),
            'GH_FILES_API_FAILURE': str(files_api_fails).lower(),
        },
        text=True,
        capture_output=True,
        check=False,
    )
    if process.returncode != 0:
        assert not output.exists()
        return 'error'
    return output.read_text(encoding='utf-8').strip().split('=', maxsplit=1)[1]


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ('changed_files', 'expected'),
    [
        ([('pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/ui/_adapter.py', '')], 'true'),
        ([('src/pydantic_clai2/web-ui/src/App.tsx', '')], 'true'),
        ([('src/pydantic_clai2/pydantic_clai2/builtin_plugins/web/app.py', '')], 'true'),
        ([('src/pydantic_clai2/pydantic_clai2/cli/web.py', '')], 'true'),
        ([('src/pydantic_clai2/scripts/check_web_assets.py', '')], 'true'),
        ([('tests/clai2/test_web_keys.py', '')], 'true'),
        ([('tests/clai2/browser/test_security.py', '')], 'true'),
        ([('docs/harness/clai2.md', '')], 'true'),
        ([('docs/web.md', '')], 'true'),
        ([('src/pydantic_clai2/web-ui-old/src/App.tsx', '')], 'false'),
        ([('tests/clai2/test_cli.py', '')], 'false'),
        ([('README.md', '')], 'false'),
        ([('src/renamed.py', 'src/pydantic_clai2/web-ui/src/App.tsx')], 'true'),
        ([('src/renamed.py', 'pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/ui/_adapter.py')], 'true'),
    ],
)
def test_detects_ui_security_paths_and_renames(
    tmp_path: Path, changed_files: list[tuple[str, str]], expected: str
) -> None:
    """Detect covered paths under current and previous filenames."""
    assert _detect(tmp_path, changed_files) == expected


def test_detection_fails_closed_when_pull_request_files_cannot_be_read(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    """Fail the detector job when GitHub cannot return the changed-file list."""
    assert _detect(tmp_path, [('README.md', '')], files_api_fails=True) == 'error'


def test_large_changed_file_list_still_detects_ui_security_paths(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    """Drain large file lists after finding a matching path to avoid SIGPIPE."""
    changed_files = [('src/pydantic_clai2/web-ui/src/App.tsx', '')] + [
        (f'unrelated/{index:04d}/' + 'x' * 90, '') for index in range(2000)
    ]

    assert _detect(tmp_path, changed_files) == 'true'

# Examples

Complete agents assembled from individual harness capabilities, written to be
read as much as run: every capability choice has the reasoning next to it, and
each example writes out its full configuration so you can copy it into your own
code and tweak it.

If you just want the assembled version, use the packaged harnesses instead
([`Coder`](../../../docs/harness/coder.md), [`Researcher`](../../../docs/harness/researcher.md)) — or run one
with zero setup: `uvx --with pydantic-ai-harness clai -a pydantic_ai_harness.coder:coder_agent`.

## Setup

From the repo root:

```bash
make install                      # or: uv sync --all-extras
uv run examples/coding_agent.py
```

Each example states its default model at the top and reads that provider's API
key from the environment (e.g. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`). Set
`PYDANTIC_AI_MODEL=provider:model` to run against a different model — you'll
then need that provider's key instead.

## The examples

| Example | What it does | Default model |
|---|---|---|
| [`coding_agent.py`](coding_agent.py) | A coding agent for the current repo: `Coder` in a local workspace that passes on `PATH`, `HOME`, `LANG`, `LC_ALL` and `LC_CTYPE` | `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5` |
| [`research_agent.py`](research_agent.py) | A web-research agent that cites every claim, built from the blocks that make up `Researcher` | `openai:gpt-5.6-sol` |

Every example exposes a `build_agent()` factory (imported by the test suite, and
handy for embedding the agent in your own code) and a `main()` that starts an
interactive session.
